title: Tribocharging of Granular Materials Dictated by Geometric and Thermoelectric Effects
authors: Donggeun Kang, Ji-Ho Mun, Seungil Baek, Jaeuk Seo, Sirichok Jungthawan, Yong Woon Kim, Yong-Hyun Kim
abstract: Tribocharging of granular materials is a widespread phenomenon ranging from volcanic eruptions and dust storms to pharmaceutical processing, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Recent thermoelectric models have provided a quantitative framework for triboelectric charge transfer, but they have difficulty accounting for charging between identical materials. In this Letter, we propose a theory of granular tribocharging based on the interplay between particle geometry and thermoelectric response. Collision-induced frictional heating produces a size-dependent temperature asymmetry between particles, generating a thermoelectric voltage that drives charge transfer. The sign of the Seebeck coefficient determines the charging polarity, while particle size and thermal properties set its magnitude. Our multi-collision theory explains the experimentally observed size- and material-dependent reversal of charging polarity, as in quartz and nylon.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive theory for tribocharging in granular materials, attributing the charge transfer to a thermoelectric voltage generated by temperature asymmetries during particle collisions. By coupling heat diffusion modeling with the Seebeck effect, the authors successfully explain complex experimental observations, such as polarity reversals dependent on both particle size and material composition.
main_problem: The underlying mechanism of tribocharging in granular materials is poorly understood, especially the size- and material-dependent reversal of charging polarity.
main_result: The authors propose a theory linking charge transfer to the thermoelectric voltage generated by size-dependent temperature asymmetries induced by frictional heating during collisions.
method: The theory models the thermal response using the heat diffusion equation solved via eigenfunction expansion, coupling this to the thermoelectric potential ($\Delta V = -S\Delta T$).
model_or_system: The system is granular materials undergoing random collisions. The model incorporates particle geometry (size $R$) and intrinsic material properties ($ho, c, k, S$) to calculate the resulting surface potential.
key_observables: Surface potential ($\Delta V$), charge transfer polarity, and surface charge density ($\sigma$).
important_parameters: Seebeck coefficient ($S$), particle size ($R$), thermal conductivity ($k$), and the Biot number ($	ext{Bi}$).
main_assumptions: Particles are idealized spheres; heat input is modeled as a localized interfacial source; charge transfer adjusts instantaneously to the thermoelectric potential.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature asymmetry leading to $\Delta V = -S\Delta T$, show how the sign of $S$ dictates charge transfer direction, and confirm that the model explains size-dependent and material-dependent polarity reversals.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the single-collision potential based on heat diffusion, then extending this to a multi-collision statistical accumulation model, and finally demonstrating how geometry and material properties govern the observed charge segregation.
why_interesting: While focused on classical solid-state physics, the coupling of non-equilibrium thermodynamics (heat diffusion) with emergent macroscopic properties (charge) shares conceptual links with open quantum systems where environmental coupling drives non-equilibrium steady states.
